MILITARY STATUS EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION PROTECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Military and Veterans Code section 394, a state statute that prohibits discrimination against a member of the military or naval forces of California or of the United States because of that membership, and that separately prohibits an employer from discharging, hindering, or otherwise penalizing an employee for performing ordered military duty, training, or drill, or for enlisting or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component. Section 394 applies to private employers as well as to state and local government employers; a violation is a misdemeanor and also gives rise to a civil claim for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. This document does not cover section 394's separate provisions addressing a uniformed member's access to public entertainment or places of amusement (subdivision (c)) or lending and financing discrimination (subdivision (f)), and it does not cover the temporary military leave-of-absence, salary-continuation, and reinstatement provisions found elsewhere in the same statutory chapter (Military and Veterans Code sections 395 through 395.08, 395.1, and 395.3), which by their own terms apply only to public employees and public agencies, not to private-sector employment. Federal reemployment and leave rights connected to military service for private-sector employees are instead addressed under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), described in this corpus's separate USERRA information sheet.

GENERAL PROHIBITION ON DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF MILITARY MEMBERSHIP
Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(a), a person may not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership, and a member of the military forces may not be prejudiced or injured by a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm in the terms, conditions, or privileges of that member's employment, position, or status, or be denied or disqualified for employment, by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(a) A person shall not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership. A member of the military forces shall not be prejudiced or injured by a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm in terms, conditions, or privileges with respect to that member’s employment, position or status or be denied or disqualified for employment by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(a), general prohibition on discrimination because of membership in the military or naval forces (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (a)'s own text does not define what conduct counts as "discriminate," "prejudiced," or "injured," does not list any example of a prohibited or permitted employment decision, and does not state any employer-size threshold or exemption. It also does not itself create a remedy or private right of action; the misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees remedy are supplied by a different subsection, (g), described in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether any specific employer decision or practice would meet subdivision (a)'s standard.

PARALLEL PROHIBITION SPECIFICALLY NAMING STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT EMPLOYERS
Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(b), an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district, may not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership, and a member of the military forces may not be prejudiced or injured by such an officer or employee in the terms, conditions, or privileges of that member's employment, appointment, position, or status, or be denied, disqualified, or discharged from that employment or position by virtue of membership or service in the military forces.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(b) An officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district shall not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership. A member of the military forces shall not be prejudiced or injured by an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district in terms, conditions, or privileges with respect to that member’s employment, appointment, position, or status or be denied or disqualified for or discharged from that employment or position by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(b), parallel prohibition naming state and local government officers and employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (b) uses different wording from subdivision (a): it names "an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district" as the regulated actor, rather than subdivision (a)'s broader "a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm." The statute's text does not state whether subdivisions (a) and (b) are meant to be mutually exclusive or overlapping as applied to a government employer, and this document does not resolve that overlap question. Subdivision (b) also does not itself state a remedy; like subdivision (a), it relies on subdivision (g) for the misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees claim.

PROTECTION FROM DISCHARGE OR HINDRANCE FOR PERFORMING MILITARY DUTY
Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(d), an employer, or an officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, may not discharge a person from employment because of the performance of ordered military duty or training, or because of membership in the military or naval forces of the state or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces, and may not hinder or prevent a person from performing military service or from attending a military encampment, drill, or instruction the person is called upon to attend, or prejudice or harm the person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment for doing so. The same subdivision separately prohibits dissuading, preventing, or stopping a person from enlisting or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component, by threatening injury to the person's employment terms, status, trade, or business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(d) An employer or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, shall not discharge a person from employment because of the performance of any ordered military duty or training or by reason of being a member of the military or naval forces of this state or of the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States, or hinder or prevent that person from performing any military service or from attending any military encampment or place of drill or instruction the person may be called upon to perform or attend by proper authority; prejudice or harm the person in any manner in the person’s terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, position, or status by reason of performance of military service or duty or attendance at military encampments or places of drill or instruction; or dissuade, prevent, or stop any person from enlistment or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States by threat or injury to the person in respect to the person’s terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, position, status, trade, or business because of enlistment or acceptance of a warrant or commission."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(d), protection from discharge or hindrance for performing military duty or seeking to enlist (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (d)'s text does not define "ordered military duty," does not state a maximum number of protected days (contrast the separate 180-calendar-day cap that section 395(a) places on a public employee's temporary military leave of absence, described in a separate clause of this document, which section 394(d) does not reference or incorporate), and does not itself describe a complaint or reinstatement procedure. It also does not state whether the discharge or hindrance must be the sole reason for the adverse action or merely a substantial or motivating factor; this document does not resolve that question from the statutory text alone.

PROTECTION OF COLLATERAL BENEFITS DURING TEMPORARY INCAPACITATION INCIDENT TO DUTY
Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(e)(1), a private employer, or an officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, may not restrict or terminate an employee's collateral benefit because of the employee's temporary incapacitation incident to duty in the National Guard, State Guard, Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component, where "temporary incapacitation" is defined as any period of incapacitation of 52 weeks or less. Section 394(e)(2) defines "benefit" for purposes of this subdivision to include, but not be limited to, health care (which may be continued at the employee's expense), life insurance, disability insurance, and seniority status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(e) (1) A private employer or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, shall not restrict or terminate any collateral benefit for employees by reason of an employee’s temporary incapacitation incident to duty in the National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States. As used in this subdivision, “temporary incapacitation” means any period of incapacitation of 52 weeks or less."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(1), protection of collateral benefits during temporary incapacitation incident to duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  "(2) As used in this subdivision, “benefit” includes, but is not limited to, health care which may be continued at the employee’s expense, life insurance, disability insurance, and seniority status."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(2), definition of "benefit" for purposes of subdivision (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (e)(1) is worded to reach a "private employer," a narrower category than the "person" language of subdivision (a) or the state/local-government language of subdivision (b); this document does not determine whether subdivision (e) also reaches state or local government employers by virtue of subdivisions (a) or (b) applying more broadly, because subdivision (e)'s own text does not say so. The 52-week definition of "temporary incapacitation" means an incapacitation lasting longer than 52 weeks falls outside this specific protection, and the statute's text does not state what protection, if any, applies beyond that point. Subdivision (e)(2)'s statement that health care "may be continued at the employee's expense" means the employer is not shown by this text to be required to pay the premium, only to permit continued coverage; the statute does not describe the continuation mechanism (for example, whether it resembles COBRA continuation) in any further detail.

MISDEMEANOR PENALTY, CIVIL DAMAGES, AND NON-EXCLUSIVE REMEDIES
Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(g), a person who violates section 394 is guilty of a misdemeanor, and a person who violates any provision of the section is also liable for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees incurred by the injured party. Section 394(h) states that the remedies provided in section 394 are not intended to be exclusive, but are in addition to remedies provided in other laws, including Civil Code sections 51 and 52.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(g) A person violating this section is guilty of a misdemeanor. In addition, a person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable for actual damages and reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the injured party."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(g) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(g), misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees remedy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  "(h) The remedies provided for in this section are not intended to be exclusive but are in addition to the remedies provided for in other laws, including Sections 51 and 52 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(h) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(h), remedies not exclusive, cumulative with other laws (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=394.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (g)'s text does not state a limitations period for the civil damages claim, does not name the court in which such a claim may be brought, does not describe a filing or notice procedure, and does not state whether "actual damages" includes noneconomic loss such as emotional distress or only economic loss. The subdivision also does not describe how a misdemeanor prosecution would be initiated, since criminal charges are ordinarily brought by a public prosecutor rather than the injured employee; section 394's text does not itself address that mechanic. Subdivision (h)'s cross-reference to Civil Code sections 51 and 52 is stated without elaborating what additional remedy those sections would add in an employment context beyond what section 394 itself provides, and this document does not independently verify Civil Code sections 51 and 52 here.

ONLY THE EMPLOYER, NOT INDIVIDUAL SUPERVISORS, MAY BE HELD LIABLE UNDER SECTION 394
In Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983 (2011), the California Court of Appeal held, as a matter of first impression, that although section 394(g) attaches liability to "a person" who violates the section, an employee who is subject to military duty or training that interrupts their work may hold their employer liable for discrimination or retaliation in violation of section 394, but may not hold an individual supervisor personally liable for acts arising out of the performance of normal management duties. The court reasoned that section 394's use of "person" is analogous to the California Fair Employment and Housing Act's use of "employer," which California courts have likewise construed not to impose individual liability on supervisors for ordinary personnel-management decisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Plaintiffs who are subject to military duty or training that interrupts their work may hold their employers, but not individuals, liable for discrimination in violation of section 394. The plaintiff employee’s target remains the employer."
  — Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983 (2011), Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983, 996 (2d Dist. 2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810679/haligowski-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This document read only Haligowski v. Superior Court in full; a CourtListener keyword search for "Military and Veterans Code" section 394 employment discrimination in California courts returned four results, and the other three (Del Monte v. Wilson, Kopp v. Fair Political Practices Commission, and In re Cox) were not read or relied on here, so this document does not state whether or how those decisions discuss section 394. The search was a single keyword search rather than a citator or cited-by analysis, so this document cannot rule out other published California appellate decisions on section 394 that did not match the search terms used. The California Supreme Court denied review of Haligowski (noted in the opinion itself), which means Haligowski remains a published, citable Court of Appeal decision, but denial of review does not itself signify Supreme Court endorsement of the reasoning, only a decision not to review it. This document does not address whether the same employer-only, not-individual, liability rule would apply to a claim brought under section 394(a) or (b) alone rather than the discharge/hindrance claim actually before the Haligowski court.

SCOPE LIMIT: THE CHAPTER'S LEAVE-OF-ABSENCE AND REINSTATEMENT PROVISIONS APPLY ONLY TO PUBLIC EMPLOYEES
Section 394 sits within the same statutory chapter (Military and Veterans Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 7) as a separate group of sections, beginning with section 395(a), that grant a temporary military leave of absence and a right of reinstatement. Unlike section 394's antidiscrimination language, section 395(a) is worded to cover only a "public employee": it entitles a public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces, the National Guard, or the Naval Militia to a temporary military leave of absence, as provided by federal law, for ordered duty not exceeding 180 calendar days including travel time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(a) Any public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces of the United States or of the National Guard or the Naval Militia is entitled to a temporary military leave of absence as provided by federal law while engaged in military duty ordered for purposes of active military training, inactive duty training, encampment, naval cruises, special exercises, or like activity, providing that the period of ordered duty does not exceed 180 calendar days, including time involved in going to and returning from that duty."
  — Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 395(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 395(a), public-employee temporary military leave of absence, 180-calendar-day cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=MVC&sectionNum=395.)

That single-fetch chapter read was not independently double-fetched or re-verified word-for-word the way section 394 and section 395(a) were, so this document does not quote those later sections and does not assert their complete or current content beyond the opening-sentence phrasing observed. This document does not identify what "as provided by federal law" in section 395(a) refers to, and does not state whether any state-law leave-of-absence or reinstatement right, parallel to section 395, exists for a private-sector employee outside of section 394 itself; private-sector federal reemployment rights connected to military service are addressed separately under USERRA in this corpus's USERRA information sheet, which this document does not restate.

expectedJSON.body: Section 394 sits within the same statutory chapter (Military and Veterans Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 7) as a separate group of sections, beginning with section 395(a), that grant a temporary military leave of absence and a right of reinstatement. Unlike section 394's antidiscrimination language, section 395(a) is worded to cover only a "public employee": it entitles a public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces, the National Guard, or the Naval Militia to a temporary military leave of absence, as provided by federal law, for ordered duty not exceeding 180 calendar days including travel time.

citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 395(a), public-employee temporary military leave of absence, 180-calendar-day cap
citations.quote: (a) Any public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces of the United States or of the National Guard or the Naval Militia is entitled to a temporary military leave of absence as provided by federal law while engaged in military duty ordered for purposes of active military training, inactive duty training, encampment, naval cruises, special exercises, or like activity, providing that the period of ordered duty does not exceed 180 calendar days, including time involved in going to and returning from that duty.
